lines.text: Detective Marcus, back on the protist beat. Part two: the last two supergroups.
Last time, we met Excavata and the SAR clade. Today: Archaeplastida, and Unikonta.
Supergroup three: Archaeplastida.
The name literally means ancient plastids. All its members share chloroplasts that trace back to one event, about a billion years ago.
A heterotrophic eukaryote engulfed a cyanobacteria like organism. Instead of being digested, it stayed, and became the chloroplast. This is the theory of endosymbiosis.
The similarities between plastids and cyanobacteria were first noticed by Schimper, in 1883.
Later, McFadden described how deeply the two partners merged: in structure, in metabolism, and in their genes. The result was a lineage of eukaryotes powered by light.
Dating that event with molecular clocks is still difficult. But every archaeplastid descends from it.
Archaeplastida has three subgroups: glaucophytes, red algae, and the green algae together with land plants.
First, the glaucophytes. Not much is known about them, except that they live near the surface of fresh water.
Their plastids, called cyanelles, keep many traits of the original cyanobacterium. The model species, Cyanophora paradoxa, helps scientists study how endosymbiosis happened.
Next, the rhodophytes, or red algae. There are at least six thousand species, mostly marine.
Some are single celled, but most are filamentous or multicellular.
Their red color comes from a pigment called phycoerythrin. The deeper they live, the darker they look. In deep water, some appear almost black.
Red algae are common in warm tropical seas, and they are economically important. They give us carrageenan and agar.
And the nori wrapped around your sushi? That is the red alga Pyropia, dried into sheets.
So that's what's been hiding in my sushi.
The third subgroup is Chloroplastida: the green algae, together with land plants.
About twelve thousand green algae species are known. They share the pigments of land plants: chlorophyll a and b, carotene, and xanthophyll.
Green algae can be motile or non motile. Most live in fresh water, but there are land and marine species too.
Tiny, free floating green algae are key oxygen producers in aquatic ecosystems.
They come in many forms: unicellular, colonial, multicellular, filamentous, and tubular.
Chlamydomonas is a single swimming cell. Volvox lives in rolling colonies. Ulva, the sea lettuce, is multicellular. And Caulerpa taxifolia is the largest single celled organism.
Think it over. What conditions could have allowed ancestral green algae to move onto land? Pause, and think.

One suggested answer: their closest living relatives, the charophytes, live in fresh water. Adapting to a dry, glaciated Earth may have produced pathways like photorespiration, helping them move onto land.
Supergroup four: Unikonta.
It is the most mixed group of all, with two major clades: Amoebozoa and Opisthokonta. Molecular studies link them, but their exact relationship is still being tested.
Amoebozoa are amoebas for all, or most, of their life cycle. They move using pseudopodia.
Most have broad, lobe shaped pseudopods. A few are filose, or reticulate.
Lobose amoebae can be naked, or covered by a glycocalyx, a barrier against their surroundings.
When food runs low, they form cysts. When conditions improve, they eat their prey by phagocytosis.
This makes them an important link in aquatic food webs.
Amoebozoa also include the fungus like slime molds, such as Physarum. The most species rich group is the plasmodial slime molds.
They live worldwide, on decaying plants, leaf litter, and tree bark. Their spores develop into a plasmodium, often yellow or orange.
The other clade, Opisthokonta, includes two protist groups: nucleariids, and choanoflagellates.
Nucleariids are filose amoebae, considered the ancestral group of fungi.
Choanoflagellates are the closest known relatives of animals. They are single celled or colonial, and live in fresh and salt water worldwide.
A collar of microvilli surrounds one flagellum. The beating flagellum creates a current, food particles are filtered onto the collar, and then eaten by phagocytosis.
Think it over. Choanoflagellates look strikingly like choanocytes, the collar cells of sponges. If they are the ancestral form, what could have pushed them to become multicellular?
And now, a real case for you to solve.
December twenty second, twenty sixteen. Eight twenty four p m. Cabucgayan, Biliran. A neighbor reports a married couple found unconscious, in their house facing the sea.
On the table: fresh oysters, puso, isaw, and a pitcher of clear water. Two unfinished plates, each with an empty oyster shell. A broken glass lies on the floor.
Nearby, an earthen jar of water smells like rotten eggs. And by the basin: empty blister packs of paracetamol.
The weather: twenty eight degrees Celsius, with eighty three percent humidity. At the hospital, the couple is stable, but still unconscious.
The epidemiologist suspects a parasitic protist. Four suspects: Plasmodium, Entamoeba, Giardia, and Pyrodinium bahamense.
Which protist is the most probable suspect, and why? Build its profile: general information, symptoms, diagnosis, and a treatment available locally.
Use the clues. Comment your suspect. I'll be reading.
Protists keep surprising scientists. New species are still waiting to be found: some harmful, some helpful, and some that may explain how animals came from a single cell.
Big things really do come in small packages.
Case closed. For now.
